summary:
Mexico has no national administrative procedure for legal gender recognition; the process is set state by state. As of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more operated one in practice without legislative enactment, and six state legislatures had enacted none at all. Only seven states extend recognition to children.

In 2022 the Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. Where no procedure exists, trans people are left carrying identity documents that contradict their lived gender, and that mismatch drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco. Recognition therefore depends on the state a person is in.

Tabasco, documented jointly by Human Rights Watch and the Community Center for Inclusion on 6 March 2024, had no legal gender-recognition procedure. There, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions.

The protective machinery is weak. More than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022, and the Tabasco material includes the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa.
tangentialFactors:
Formal rights and their enforcement diverge. Analysis published by Caroline Beer on the LSE USAPP blog (22 November 2024) found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist on paper but are rarely enjoyed in practice; Beer stated explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people in Mexico are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Killings of trans people continue and have drawn public protest. The Associated Press reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening period of that year, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, which triggered LGBTQ+ outrage and street demonstrations. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and the murder of LGBTI+ defenders had increased over the previous year. Transgender Europe monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico from 2008 to September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a total second only to Brazil's 100.

Legislative and oversight responses exist alongside that record. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide; the law is named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists quoted at the time described the measure as critical to their feeling safe in the capital. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking recognition proceed under their own state's rules. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 states operate legislated administrative procedures, two run a procedure in practice without legislative enactment, and six legislatures have enacted none; the same dispatch called on the states that lack procedures to adopt them and warned that implementation differs sharply from one state to another.

Supreme Court guidelines issued in 2022 bind the states and extended recognition to minors, while only seven states currently extend recognition to children and adolescents. Where a resident's state has no procedure, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation, as Human Rights Watch warned on 31 March 2025.

The Tabasco findings describe the resident position in detail. Without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. Delays and refusals in name and gender recognition leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory does not identify which six state legislatures have enacted no recognition procedure, which two operate a procedure without enactment, or which seven extend recognition to children. Only Tabasco is confirmed as lacking a procedure, on the 6 March 2024 reporting.

Unresolved: whether the Supreme Court's 2022 binding guidelines have been enforced against a legislature that has not enacted a procedure is not sourced here, nor is the practical effect of the Inter-American Court's requirement on states without domestic procedures.

Not sourced: whether any state recognition procedure is open to foreign nationals, and how gender markers on foreign passports are treated at entry or by police. Entry, visa and border-screening rules for trans visitors are not covered by this inventory.

Unresolved: the incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco are characterised only as document-mismatch discrimination, without dates, complainants or outcomes. The August 2023 Villahermosa killing is given without any statement on whether a case was opened or resolved.
